item.title: Code uniqueness of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters in spatial chromatic model
item.description: arXiv:2610.37395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spatial chromatic model (SCM) is a novel entity-oriented spatial data model proposed in recent years. Spatial tessellations formed by SCM have been applied in preliminary analyses of spatial point pattern recognition,spatial topology, and Voronoi diagram generation. Unlike previous spatial tessellation models, a key feature of SCM is that each subspace (cell) possesses a chromatic code, which serves as the foundation for various theoretical analyses and applications of SCM. The uniqueness of cell cluster codes in SCM constitutes an important property of the model. Previous studies have demonstrated the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 2-cell and 3-cell connected disjoint clusters. Building on this analysis of connected cluster code characteristics, this paper proves the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters. The proof results and the new concepts introduced in this study help further refine the spatial chromatic model and provide a theoretical foundation for its subsequent applications.
item.dc:creator: Weining Zhu

item.title: Realizing graph automorphisms as geometric symmetries of straight line drawings
item.description: arXiv:2610.36394v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a finite graph $G$, we characterize the automorphisms and automorphism groups of $G$ that can be realized as geometric symmetries and symmetry groups of straight line drawings of $G$ in the plane. In doing so, we correct a previous version of this characterization from the literature. As an application, we show that the graphs recently constructed by the first two authors to disprove the Polycirculant Conjecture, which have orders $16{,}464^k$ for each positive integer $k$, are the first known vertex-transitive graphs with no non-trivial realizable geometric symmetries. We also construct infinite families of graphs that exhibit all possible kinds of geometric symmetry.
item.dc:creator: Saul D. Freedman, Melissa Lee, Dragan Maru\v{s}i\v{c}, Toma\v{z} Pisanski

item.title: On surfaces, that fill the space
item.description: arXiv:2610.36766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The article is devoted to the construction of dimension-raising maps of cubes with the highest possible Holder exponent. In particular, a square-to-cube mapping with a Holder exponent of $2/3$ is constructed, which is a solution to the V.I.Arnold problem.
item.dc:creator: E. V. Shchepin

item.title: Prismatoid Band-Unfolding Revisited
item.description: arXiv:2603.09813v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It remains unknown if every prismatoid has a nonoverlapping edge-unfolding, a special case of the long-unsolved "D\"urer's problem." Recently nested prismatoids have been settled [Rad24] by mixing (in some sense) the two natural unfoldings, petal-unfolding and band-unfolding. Band-unfolding fails due to a specific counterexample [O'R13b]. The main contribution of this paper is a characterization when a band-unfolding of a nested prismatoid does in fact result in a nonoverlapping unfolding. In particular, we show that the mentioned counterexample is in a sense the only possible counterexample. Although this result does not expand the class of shapes known to have an edge-unfolding, its proof expands our understanding in several ways, developing tools that may help resolve the non-nested case.
item.dc:creator: Joseph O'Rourke

item.title: A Tight 3-Approximation for Fair $k$-Means
item.description: arXiv:2609.07974v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fairness in clustering has attracted sustained research interest, motivated by the need to ensure equitable representation of protected groups in machine learning applications. We study fair $k$-means clustering in Euclidean space, where the proportion of each protected group in every cluster must lie within specified lower and upper bounds. These constraints make it challenging to determine both cluster centers and point assignments. Our algorithm first splits the input into many small fair clusters and then merges them into $k$ clusters with a weighted $k$-means algorithm. The merge is cheap only when the small clusters do not move points away from their optimal centers, so we add a displacement penalty to the split, which charges each point for how far the small clusters move it. Given a $\rho$-approximate algorithm for weighted $k$-means and any $\epsilon>0$, our algorithm returns a fractional solution whose cost is at most $3\rho+\epsilon$ times the optimal integral fair cost. With a PTAS as the subroutine, the approximation ratio becomes $3+O(\epsilon)$, improving the previous factor of $5+O(\epsilon)$. This ratio is the best possible: unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves the ratio $3-\delta$ for any fixed $\delta>0$, even in one dimension. The solution satisfies all fairness constraints exactly and can be rounded to an integral assignment with a bounded additive violation of fairness and no increase in cost. The same approximation guarantee extends to the $k$-sparse Wasserstein barycenter problem.
item.dc:creator: Kangke Cheng, Guanlin Mo, Shihong Song, Hu Ding

item.title: Polynomial and Hyperplane Avoidance over the Integers with Applications to Integer-Point Counting
item.description: arXiv:2411.07030v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the \emph{Polynomial Avoidance Problem}: given a finite collection $F \subseteq Z[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of nonzero polynomials, find a vector $x \in Z^n$ of minimum $\ell_p$-norm such that $f(x)\neq0$ for every $f \in F$. Each polynomial is given sparsely as a list of its nonzero terms. The affine special case is the \emph{Hyperplane Avoidance Problem}. This special case arises in Barvinok-type algorithms for counting integer points in polyhedra, when certain rational generating functions must be evaluated at a removable singularity. Our main results are as follows: 1) Let $D:=\sum_{f\in F} \text{deg} f$. Every instance admits a feasible vector $x$ satisfying \[ \|x\|_1 \leq \min\left\{D,\frac{D+n}{2}\right\}. \] This bound is tight. Such a vector can be found by a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in $D$ and the sparse encoding length of the input. Our proof uses a new algorithmic variant of the \emph{Combinatorial Nullstellensatz}; 2) In the affine case, with $m$ input polynomials, such a vector can be constructed by a fast deterministic polynomial-time algorithm using $O(nm)$ arithmetic operations. For the homogeneous case, Barvinok's original approach provides only the weaker guarantee $\|x\|_1 = O((nm)^{n-1})$; 3) The problem is NP-hard for every $p\in R_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}$, even for homogeneous linear forms; 4) As an application, we improve the complexity bound for counting integer points in general rational polytopes. We also improve the bound for polyhedra of bounded codimension; this includes the counting version of the \emph{Unbounded Subset-Sum} problem as a special case.
item.dc:creator: Grigorii Dakhno, Dmitry Gribanov, Nikita Kasianov, Anastasiia Kats, Andrey Kupavskii, Nikita Kuz'min, Stanislav Moiseev

item.title: On the Vertices of Delta-modular Polyhedra
item.description: arXiv:2506.12774v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $P$ be a polytope defined by the system $A x \leq b$, where $A \in R^{m \times n}$, $b \in R^m$, and $\text{rank}(A) = n$. We give a short geometric proof of the following tight upper bound on the number of vertices of $P$: $$ n! \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\text{average}}} \cdot \text{vol}(B_2) \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi n}} \cdot \left(\frac{2 \pi}{e}\right)^{n/2} \cdot n^{n/2} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\text{average}}}, $$ where $\Delta$ is the maximum absolute value of $n \times n$ subdeterminants of $A$, and $\Delta_{\text{average}}$ is the average absolute value of subdeterminants of $A$ corresponding to a triangulation of $P$'s normal fan. Assuming that $A$ is integer, such polyhedra are called $\Delta$-modular polyhedra. Note that in the integer case, the bound can be simplified via the inequality $\Delta_{\text{average}} \geq \Delta_{\min} \geq 1$, where $\Delta_{\min}$ is the minimum absolute value of subdeterminants of $A$ corresponding to feasible bases of $A x \leq b$. For this, we prove and use a symmetric variant of Macbeath's theorem. Additionally, we give a direct argument based on prior results in the field, showing that the graph diameter of $P$ is bounded by $O\bigl(n^3 \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\min}} \cdot \ln (n \frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\min}}) \bigr)$. Thus, both characteristic of $P$ are linear in $\Delta/\Delta_{\min}$. From an algorithmic perspective, we demonstrate that: Given $A \in Q^{m \times n}$, $b \in Q^m$, and an initial feasible solution to $A x \leq b$, the convex hull of $P$ can be constructed in $O(n)^{n/2} \cdot m^2 \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\Delta_{\text{average}}}$ operations. For simple polyhedra, the dependence on $m$ reduces to linear; Given $A \in Z^{m \times n}$ and $b \in Q^m$, the number $|P \cap Z^n|$ can be computed in $O(n)^n \cdot \frac{\Delta^4}{\Delta_{\text{average}}}$ arithmetic operations.
item.dc:creator: Bludov Mikhail, Gribanov Dmitry, Klimenko Maxim, Kupavskii Andrey, L\'angi Zsolt, Rogozin Alexander, Voronov Vsevolod

item.title: RPT*: Global Planning with Probabilistic Terminals for Target Search in Complex Environments
item.description: arXiv:2601.12701v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Routing problems such as Hamiltonian Path Problem (HPP), seek a path to visit all the vertices in a graph while minimizing the path cost. This paper studies a variant, HPP with Probabilistic Terminals (HPP-PT), where each vertex has a probability representing the likelihood that the robot's path terminates there, and the objective is to minimize the expected path cost. HPP-PT arises in target object search, where a mobile robot must visit all candidate locations to find an object, and prior knowledge of the object's location is expressed as vertex probabilities. While routing problems have been studied for decades, few of them consider uncertainty as required in this work. The challenge lies not only in optimality ordering the vertices, as in standard HPP, but also in handling history dependency: the expected path cost depends on the order in which vertices were previously visited. This makes many existing methods inefficient or inapplicable. To address the challenge, we propose a search-based approach RPT* with solution optimality guarantees, which leverages dynamic programming in a new state space to bypass the history dependency and novel heuristics to speed up the computation. Building on RPT*, we design a Hierarchical Autonomous Target Search (HATS) system that combines RPT* with either Bayesian filtering for lifelong target search with noisy sensors, or autonomous exploration to find targets in unknown environments. Experiments in both simulation and real robot show that our approach can naturally balance between exploitation and exploration, thereby finding targets more quickly on average than baseline methods.
item.dc:creator: Yunpeng Lyu, Chao Cao, Ji Zhang, Howie Choset, Zhongqiang Ren
